item.title: Xi to attend APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, related events in Shenzhen
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 01:00:00
The APEC "China Year" logo decoration is seen at Qianhai Stone Park in Shenzhen. China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19, 2026. Photo: Xinhua The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19 under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." President Xi Jinping will chair the meeting and deliver remarks. The APEC CEO Summit will be held in Shenzhen from November 17 to 18 under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together." President Xi will attend the opening ceremony and deliver a keynote speech. President Xi will hold a welcome banquet for participating leaders and representatives, and hold bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the meeting. From the banks of Shanghai's Huangpu River in 2001 to the shores of Beijing's Yanqi Lake in 2014, and now to the coast of the South China Sea in Shenzhen, the three host cities string together a 25-year journey of mutual achievement between China and the Asia-Pacific. As China takes the baton as APEC host for the third time after a 12-year interval, the country is expected to play a more pivotal and constructive role in rallying regional centripetal force, bringing much-needed certainty, and turning the blueprint of building an Asia-Pacific community into concrete action amid an increasingly turbulent global environment, scholars and attendees said. "We look forward to working with all parties to adopt the Shenzhen Declaration at next week's APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, and achieve practical outcomes in areas that are vital for both regional and global economic growth, such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, and artificial intelligence," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Friday, when asked about China's expectations for the key outcomes of the APEC summit. From learning the rules to shaping the agenda Looking back at China's three APEC host years reveals a clear evolutionary trajectory in China's role in the multilateral cooperation mechanism, from an active participant and a key initiator to now a provider of solutions to the defining challenges of our times, Liu Chenyang, director of the APEC Study Center at Nankai University, told the Global Times. This three-city relay also marks China's transition from "integrating into the Asia-Pacific" to "actively shaping globalization to shouldering the responsibility of leading it," underscoring the country's growing and uniquely constructive role in Asia-Pacific cooperation, analysts noted. When China hosted the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shanghai in 2001, the country was preparing to join the World Trade Organization (WTO), and APEC provided a platform for China to familiarize itself with international economic and trade rules. By the time Beijing hosted the meeting in 2014, the meeting helped bring the proposed Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) back to the center of discussions, Liu said. Now, as China prepares to host APEC for a third time, the meeting is taking shape against a markedly different regional and global economic landscape - characterized by rising unilateralism, trade protectionism, "small yard, high fence" decoupling attempts, supply chain fragmentation, and geopolitical turbulence. The more turbulent the global landscape becomes, the more indispensable China's role is in providing platforms for high-level dialogue through its diplomacy as host and injecting much-needed certainty into the Asia-Pacific, analysts said, while predicting that the meeting will put greater emphasis on advancing a shared vision for the Asia-Pacific's future. As the highest-level, broadest, and most influential economic cooperation mechanism in the Asia-Pacific, APEC carries forward the momentum of regional integration. The mechanism itself has also arrived at a significant juncture for institutional development. The 2020 Putrajaya Vision set out the goal of building an open, dynamic, resilient and peaceful Asia-Pacific community by 2040. The 2021 Aotearoa Plan of Action then established a framework for collective progress reviews at five-year intervals. This makes 2026 an important moment to assess how far the 21 members - accounting for about 62 percent of global GDP and roughly half of global trade - have moved from broad commitments toward concrete action against protectionism and uncertainty over global supply chains, Yang Jiemian, chairman of the Academic Affairs Council of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Global Times. The Shenzhen meeting is not only a major institutional milestone for the mid-term review of the Putrajaya Vision, but also an opportunity to connect China's domestic reform and opening-up agenda with regional cooperation, Yang said. Navigating headwinds with 'Chinese solutions' The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting has set three priorities, namely openness, innovation, and cooperation. This year's APEC CEO Summit will also feature discussions on a range of topics, including the development of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, artificial intelligence, the digital economy, the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and sustainable development. Those settings directly address the pressing question of where Asia-Pacific development should be heading, and how to revitalize the region's economies and bridge development gaps. Leaders across the 21 APEC economies are bringing pragmatic expectations to Shenzhen, with bilateral and multilateral interactions among major powers also being closely watched as an opportunity to foster a new model of major-country relations. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said that the advantage of these meetings is that participants are free to raise issues "directly and frankly," according to a Reuters report. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called for stable regional trade and cooperation on emerging technologies, including AI. Meanwhile, New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon underscored practical steps to make trade easier and less costly. Analysts said that in a cautious global climate, a high-level, broadly representative dialogue hosted by China provides essential certainty—helping member economies calibrate their judgments, reduce miscalculations, and demonstrate a shared willingness to tackle challenges through cooperation rather than fragmentation. Jayant Menon, visiting senior fellow at ISEAS under the Yusof Ishak Institute, said that preserving a rules-based multilateral trading system should be a central message of the meeting. "The key message that should come out of the APEC meeting, from both ASEAN and China, is that a rules-based multilateral trading system must be preserved at all costs," Menon told the Global Times. Despite the complexity of the regional landscape, practical interests continue to bring economies to the APEC table. Political and security differences have not disappeared, but trade, investment, technology and economic resilience remain areas where cooperation is widely sought, Lü Xiang, research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times. He stressed that Shenzhen offers more than a venue for diplomatic discussions. Its development provides a concrete example of how openness, industrial upgrading and innovation can reinforce one another, as China seeks to turn its vision of an Asia-Pacific community into action, Lü said. Enrique Dussel Peters, a professor at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, suggested that a global value chain perspective could offer a more practical way forward, allowing economies to deepen cooperation in areas such as auto parts, automobiles, electronics, telecommunications and agriculture through trade, foreign direct investment and research and development. "China can and will play a critical role," Dussel Peters told the Global Times. He noted that China had become an increasingly significant partner for APEC economies across a wide range of fields, including culture, education, science and technology, trade and investment. In the first three quarters of 2026, China's trade with other APEC economies reached 24.07 trillion yuan ($3.6 trillion), surging 23.9 percent year-on-year and accounting for 60.3 percent of China's total foreign trade.

item.title: Chinese industrial advances fuel Jiaolong's deep-sea upgrades
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 00:55:00
China's manned submersible Jiaolong is recovered aboard its mother ship, Deep Sea No. 1, after completing its 476th dive on November 3, 2026. Photo: Feng Fan/Global Times For the pilots and researchers aboard Deep Sea No. 1, a busy stretch at sea can mean sending Jiaolong on dives lasting around 10 hours, day after day. Keeping the Chinese manned submersible working at that pace has become easier as new batteries last longer, domestic thrusters run more quietly and equipment needs less maintenance. The research vessel is now in the South Pacific on China Deep Ocean Affairs Administration's Cruise DY100 scientific expedition, during which Jiaolong has explored sites in the Philippine Basin, the Ontong Java Plateau and the Caroline Basin. With 478 dives completed, the submersible is approaching another milestone: its 500th descent. Behind that rising tally is a series of upgrades that offers a close look at how advances across Chinese industry are reaching the deep sea. Interviews aboard Deep Sea No. 1 show how longer equipment life and lower operating costs are allowing Jiaolong to undertake more missions and encouraging more research institutions to use it. China's first independently designed and integrated deep-sea manned submersible has recently been fitted with high-energy-density, oil-immersed lithium battery packs, higher-resolution cameras and domestically developed direct-drive, low-noise DC thrusters. For those working with Jiaolong, the benefits are apparent both underwater and in the cost of getting there. A battery change with wider benefits "When Jiaolong used silver-zinc batteries, a battery pack might last only a year and could be used just 30 times after activation," Jiaolong pilot Qi Haibin told the Global Times. "After switching to the new lithium battery packs, the service life increased from one year to five years, and the number of uses rose from 30 to 750." That change has altered the economics of a research dive. According to a researcher aboard Deep Sea No. 1, the old silver-zinc battery packs cost an average of about 6 million yuan each, with prices fluctuating alongside global silver prices. Spread across their limited number of uses, that meant a battery cost of roughly 200,000 yuan ($29,982.08) for a single dive, before other expenses were considered. The expense discouraged some research institutions from using Jiaolong for deep-sea exploration. The switch to lithium batteries has sharply reduced the battery cost per dive, helping bring the total cost of a dive down to around half its previous level and drawing more institutions into Jiaolong's scientific expeditions, the researcher said. The gains reflect a connection between a highly specialized research vehicle and a much larger industrial sector. Jiaolong's batteries have demanding requirements, but the advances supporting their development have taken place alongside the rapid growth of China's commercial battery industry. "The overall development of China's battery industry has undoubtedly provided important support for Jiaolong's lithium-ion battery upgrade," a researcher aboard Deep Sea No. 1 told the Global Times. They said the submersible requires greater safety and energy density than conventional lithium batteries, while the underlying technology has advanced in step with that of other manufacturers in the market. The scale of that industrial development is reflected in an International Energy Agency commentary published on September 7, titled "The rise of lithium-ion batteries." China accounts for 85 percent of global lithium-ion battery production, and its two largest battery producers together contribute more than half of global output, the commentary said. Aboard Jiaolong, the significance of those wider advances is practical: a longer-lasting power source means a lower battery bill spread across many more missions. Combined with higher energy density, it helps sustain the repeated dives required by a busy scientific expedition. Homegrown technology at work While the battery upgrade has benefited from progress across a large commercial industry, other changes aboard Jiaolong have come from developing domestic alternatives to equipment affected by overseas export restrictions. A researcher aboard Deep Sea No. 1 told the Global Times that Chinese-made components have replaced imported equipment in the buoyancy adjustment system and hydraulic power unit. Domestically produced buoyancy materials have also replaced imported ones. The replacements have matched or exceeded the performance of the original equipment, they said. The propulsion system shows what that improvement means during a dive. According to Qi, the new domestic thrusters produce substantially less underwater noise, allowing acoustic equipment to pick up signals more clearly and creating a more comfortable working environment for the pilots. The difference continues after the submersible returns to its mother ship. "Previously, we had to maintain and service the thrusters on every expedition," Qi said. "Since replacing them with domestically produced thrusters, they have been virtually maintenance-free." With less servicing required and equipment able to serve more missions, the upgrades are making Jiaolong better suited to sustained scientific work. That capability is developing as China pursues a broader effort to expand its marine economy while strengthening protection of the ocean environment. At a press conference on November 3, 2026, Ma Weichen, an official at the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), said China would continue to focus on new technologies, new industries and new areas for development to advance the high-quality development of its marine economy. The priorities include tackling major marine technological challenges, developing more advanced equipment and supporting emerging industries, Ma said. China will also take an integrated approach to protection, development and utilization across nearshore waters, the open ocean, polar regions and the deep sea. Its gross ocean product is expected to exceed 13 trillion yuan by 2030, he said. The policy emphasis on protection is accompanied by continued efforts to survey marine ecosystems. An October 22 report jointly released by the NDRC and the Ministry of Natural Resources cited coral reef ecological surveys of Tiexian Jiao, Niu'e Jiao and Huangyan Dao among China's achievements in marine conservation since the start of the 14th Five-Year Plan period. The report said China had designated 151,000 square kilometers of marine areas within ecological conservation redlines and established 352 marine and coastal protected areas. It also highlighted the establishment of the Huangyan Dao National-Level Nature Reserve and the issuance of management measures for it. Other achievements included working to expand the existing World Heritage site for migratory bird habitats along China's Yellow Sea-Bohai Gulf coast and completing the country's first national marine disaster risk survey. Overall, marine environmental quality had improved markedly and ecological protection had made continued progress, the report said. For the team aboard Deep Sea No. 1, the change in Jiaolong's working life is recorded dive by dive. Pilot Zhang Yi noted that the submersible began its 1,000-meter-class sea trials in 2009 and completed its 300th dive in August 2024. In little more than two years since then, the tally has risen to 478. As Jiaolong moves toward its 500th dive, the benefits of its upgrades reach beyond the submersible. For research institutions once deterred by the cost, they mean more chances to take their questions to the seabed.

item.title: Mutual growth of foreign firms, Chinese market is setting an example for openness in the Asia-Pacific: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 00:35:00
Lujiazui Photo:VCG In recent days, new developments of two long-established multinational corporations in the Chinese market have drawn the attention of Bloomberg, Reuters and other international media outlets. In October, German car brand Volkswagen saw its new-energy vehicle (NEV) deliveries in China surge by nearly 350 percent year-on-year, exceeding 28,000 units - a new monthly record. Meanwhile, US financial firm Citigroup views Chinese enterprises "going global" as a significant growth opportunity, with its China-related business posting double-digit growth for many consecutive years. For this manufacturing giant and this Wall Street bank, what they gained in China are more than just orders, but greater capabilities. While it was once common to hear that foreign firms viewed China merely as a "contract manufacturing hub," they now prefer to view the country as a vibrant "innovation workshop" - an environment where companies from diverse backgrounds engage in healthy competition and mutual learning, driving both technological iteration and the enhancement of global competitiveness. As one of the first multinational corporations to enter the Chinese market, Volkswagen must have gained a profound understanding of the unique value this market holds. Faced with a 30-percent decline in vehicle deliveries during the first three quarters of this year, the company chose to partner with XPeng to co-develop an all-new electronic and electrical architecture, collaborated with Horizon Robotics to address gaps in its intelligent driving capabilities, and established its largest R&D hub outside of Germany in Hefei. The intense competitive landscape and rapidly evolving consumer demands in China are compelling a century-old automotive giant like Volkswagen to continuously recalibrate its strategy and strengthen its core competencies, ensuring it avoids the risk of "atrophy" in the face of global competition. More importantly, the significance of the Chinese market for corporate development has long transcended the notion of a mere "fitness regimen." An increasing number of multinational corporations have completed a comprehensive evolution in China, ranging from technical adaptation and trial-and-error experimentation with business models to the complete restructuring of their operational systems. The new products, technologies, and business models refined here have not only enabled these firms to secure a firm foothold in China but have also been exported to global markets, granting them a distinct, competitive edge on the international stage. This transition from simply "benefiting in China" to "growing up in China" represents one of the most vivid new opportunities that the process of Chinese modernization offers to the global economy. This phenomenon, where a company coexists and co-develops with the market, is an inevitable outcome of the ongoing evolution of the Chinese innovation ecosystem. Take Volkswagen's transformation as an example: through partnerships with local firms, the company has become deeply embedded in the innovation network of China's NEV industry, rapidly addressing its own capability gaps for the era of intelligent mobility. The mature, refined technical solutions developed here are now being considered to upgrade vehicle models back in Europe. There are many more similar stories: Adient has rolled out product plans developed in its Chongqing R&D center to its 180 manufacturing sites worldwide, while Siemens Healthineers has exported over 150 products manufactured locally in China to more than 150 countries and regions. "What is learned in China is being monetized globally" - this has become a shared consensus among multinational corporate executives in their private discussions. Even more noteworthy is that a number of service-oriented multinational corporations are upgrading their own operational capabilities as they follow the global expansion of Chinese industries. Citigroup's strategic shift serves as a prime example: While foreign banks previously entered China primarily to serve multinational firms expanding into the Chinese market, they must now grasp the global strategic logic of Chinese new-energy enterprises, navigate the financial flow regulations of cross-border e-commerce, and tailor their services to the localized operational needs of Chinese companies in emerging markets. These capabilities, honed within the Chinese market, have, in turn, become unique advantages that allow these institutions to broaden their service reach on a global scale. This two-way empowerment has moved beyond the traditional, one-way flow of expertise from foreign firms to China, fostering a new landscape where Chinese and foreign enterprises learn from and support one another as they jointly explore global markets. Viewed through the lens of the 2026 APEC meeting in Shenzhen, the symbiotic practices currently unfolding in the Chinese market serve as a compelling illustration of the three key priorities championed by this year's APEC: openness, innovation, and cooperation. Industrial interaction within the Chinese market has transcended traditional frameworks; market participants from diverse backgrounds no longer function merely as isolated links in a supply chain. Instead, they engage in deep collaboration within an open innovation ecosystem - learning from one another through robust competition, jointly refining new technologies and business models, and ultimately cultivating fresh, globally-oriented competitiveness. This pragmatic experience, forged within the Chinese market, offers a tangible, actionable model for the Asia-Pacific region as it seeks to dismantle technical barriers, strengthen industrial chain resilience, and achieve more inclusive, shared prosperity. Today's global economy remains overshadowed by geopolitical conflicts, rising protectionism, and lackluster growth momentum. Many are anxious about the rhetoric surrounding "decoupling" and "severing supply chains" and concerned about the fragmentation of global markets. As a pivotal pole in the global economic landscape characterized by both substantial scale and a dynamic capacity for innovation, China neither forms exclusive, closed-off circles nor seeks a "winner-takes-all" unipolar advantage. Instead, through the continuous opening of its market and its commitment to innovation-driven development, China provides a platform for enterprises from all nations to grow together. As successive waves of multinational corporations return to the global marketplace, armed with new capabilities honed in China, they bring with them not only more efficient technologies and business models, but also a fundamental development philosophy that openness fosters progress, and cooperation catalyzes innovation. This represents the long-term value that the Chinese market contributes to the global economy - a value that transcends short-term gains.

item.title: China, South Korea eye closer ties during FM talks
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 00:14:00
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, meets with South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun in Beijing on November 13, 2026. Photo: Chinese Foreign Ministry China and South Korea are neighbors that cannot be moved away, and deepening good-neighborly ties is the right choice for both countries, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun during talks in Beijing on Friday, calling for closer cooperation in a wide range of areas from artificial intelligence (AI) to biomedicine. During the talks, Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that the successful reciprocal visits by the two heads of state since late last year have put China-South Korea relations back on the right track of improvement. China has always attached great importance to China-South Korea relations and is ready to work with the South Korean side to further enhance mutual trust, expand cooperation in emerging fields such as AI, biomedicine, green and low-carbon development, and the silver economy on the basis of traditional cooperation, cultivate new engines of economic growth, and continuously expand common interests, Wang said. For his part, Cho said that since the reciprocal visits by heads of state of the two countries, bilateral ties have recovered and advanced. The sharp rise in trade volume and people-to-people exchanges demonstrates that the important consensus reached by the two leaders has been fully implemented, Cho said, according to a statement released by the Chinese Foreign Ministry. The talks came just days before the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting scheduled for next week in Shenzhen. During the talks, Wang said that the South Korean side successfully hosted the APEC meeting last year, and China believes it will also contribute to the APEC meeting in Shenzhen. Cho said that the South Korean side wishes APEC's "China Year" a success, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. Yang Xiyu, a senior research fellow at the China Institute of International Studies, told the Global Times on Friday that the Cho's visit to Beijing continues the momentum of sustained engagement between the two countries. "It will help translate the consensus reached in previous talks into concrete action, while underscoring the continuity and pragmatism of their diplomatic efforts," Yang said. Highlighting the growing interactions between the two sides, this marks the second round of talks between the two foreign ministers in about three months. They last held talks in Seoul on August 19. Meanwhile, bilateral trade volume has hit a new high this year, and people-to-people exchanges are expected to reach 10 million visits. South Korea's exports to China surged 133.6 percent year-on-year to $26.98 billion in October, exceeding $20 billion for the fifth consecutive month, according to South Korean official data. Industry tracker Flight Master told the Global Times recently that Chinese mainland flights to South Korea led all overseas routes in October, hitting 114.5 percent of pre-pandemic levels and surpassing volumes seen in the same month of 2019. The growing air connectivity between China and South Korea has coincided with a surge in people-to-people exchanges as bilateral ties have warmed. People-to-people and cultural exchanges between the two countries are the social foundation of bilateral relations, helping to bring the two peoples closer and enhance mutual understanding and trust, Yang said, adding that growing people-to-people exchanges between China and South Korea also help steer bilateral ties toward more stable, pragmatic and sustainable development. Nearly three-quarters of South Koreans support developing relations with China, while more than 80 percent back bilateral economic and trade cooperation, according to a Gallup Korea survey commissioned by the Chinese Embassy in South Korea that was released on October 30. China-South Korea relations are extending toward more forward-looking and diversified industrial cooperation, which not only further taps the complementarity of the two countries' industrial strengths but also injects new growth momentum into bilateral relations, Yang said.

item.title: Wuhan school introduces screen-free tutoring, pupils found more focused in classes
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 23:51:00
Students at Wuhan Optics Valley International School attended classes without watching any screens on November 11 in Wuhan, Central China's Hubei Province. Students at Wuhan Optics Valley International School attended classes without watching any screens on November 11 in Wuhan, Central China's Hubei Province, and they followed the teachers' gestures and narrations closely. This is the second month the school has held screen-free classes for an entire day. Since September 1, the school has let six grades take turns to have one day with no power points projected onto screens. Students had to learn face-to-face, using only their books, the blackboard, and other printed materials. Zhai Xiaomeng, a teacher for the fourth grade, prepared her classes using an interactive approach. Zhai was quoted as saying that power points were more colorful and students had got used to them, but since the screen-free day was introduced, she decided to slow down the tutoring rhythm and arranged writing ideas on the blackboard. Students had more opportunities to think over story plots by discussing them in teams, and Zhai was able to capture their learning feedback in a timely manner. "In a classroom without electronic screens, I can concentrate well by looking at the teacher and the blackboard," said Tian Yixin, a student at the school. One of the staff members in charge of the campaign said that the aims of the screen-free day were to protect students' eyesight, reduce the strain of prolonged screen time, encourage teachers to think out of the box in terms of their teaching approaches and to help students get more focused on learning and thinking. "After two months of implementing the 'Eye Protection Screen-Off Day,' we have found that students' concentration in class has improved, and they have developed the habit of thinking calmly and independently. Teachers' blackboard writing and lesson design abilities have greatly improved, and there has been an increase in in-depth face-to-face interaction between teachers and students," the staff member said. Global Times

item.title: Analysis: After Jensen Huang's resignation, global chip sector may enter a new period of both intense competition and vast opportunities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 23:00:00
Jensen Huang. Photo: VCG The sudden departure of Jensen Huang, who led Nvidia for 33 years and is widely regarded as an iconic figure in the global artificial intelligence (AI) industry, has drawn widespread attention from the global technology community and financial markets. What potential impact could his departure have on Nvidia's business strategy, the US AI industry ecosystem and the global competitive landscape for computing power? In interviews with the Global Times, experts said that the global chip industry could enter a new period of intense competition - like the "Warring States period" in Chinese history, with some chipmakers poised to seize fresh opportunities to expand their footprint and secure spots in more customers' supply chains. Challenges for corporate governance Some analysts believe that Huang's departure could pose challenges to Nvidia's corporate governance and strategic continuity. Liu Dian, an associate research fellow at the China Institute of Fudan University, told the Global Times that Huang's role at Nvidia went far beyond day-to-day management. For years, he had played a central role in shaping the company's technological direction, building its industry ecosystem, coordinating supply chains, and communicating with global customers and policymakers. Such a highly centralized, founder-led leadership model would be difficult to fully replicate in a short period of time, Liu Dian said. "The real period to watch is not just the next few quarters of financial performance, but the execution of Nvidia's strategy over the next one to three years." According to Liu Dian, key questions include whether Nvidia can maintain its rapid pace of product development, continue coordinating with advanced packaging providers, memory suppliers, foundries and data center customers, and sustain its competitive advantages in the Compute Unified Device Architecture ecosystem and hardware-software integration. "Huang's departure does not mean Nvidia's technological leadership will immediately be shaken, but it does mean that capital markets will increasingly shift their focus from confidence in the founder's judgment to a closer examination of the company's governance structures, management team and cash flow," Liu Dian said. Liu Shaoshan, director of the Embodied AI Center at the Shenzhen Institute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics for Society, shared a similar view. He said Huang's greatest contribution was not merely developing industry-leading GPUs, but, more importantly, building a comprehensive AI computing ecosystem through CUDA. "This technological barrier will not disappear with his departure, but his strategic leadership and ability to integrate industry resources will be difficult to replace. Nvidia will lose its central pillar of leadership," Liu Shaoshan said. Impact on US AI investment As a key player in driving the expansion of global AI infrastructure, Nvidia faces growing uncertainty over its future direction following Huang's departure, with the potential implications for the US AI industry also drawing attention from foreign media in recent days. Reuters reported that as Huang stepped down on Thursday, investors' biggest fears were as much about the future of the multitrillion-dollar company as its ability and willingness to continue bankrolling the AI boom. On Thursday, Fortune magazine cited an analyst as saying that "NVIDIA's leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom." The report noted that Nvidia has become the "central bank" of the AI industry, providing financing to dozens of other companies. Given the importance of spending on AI and data centers to the broader US economy, the potential impact of Nvidia's leadership shake-up should not be underestimated. An Bo, a President's Chair Professor and Head of Division of Artificial Intelligence at the College of Computing and Data Science of Nanyang Technological University, told the Global Times that turmoil at Nvidia could amplify existing concerns over investment returns in the US AI industry, making financing more expensive and project approvals more cautious. This could, in turn, delay data center construction, chip purchases and model training plans. AI computing cloud providers and small and medium-sized AI model companies that rely on continuous financing would likely be the first to feel the impact, An Bo said. Major technology companies, however, still have cash flow, existing computing resources and long-term contracts to support their operations. As a result, the more likely consequences would be slower expansion, greater concentration of resources among a handful of tech giants, and a stronger emphasis on efficiency and commercial returns in investment decisions. Reuters also reported that the worry in the market is that the stakes are far higher and that if Nvidia — under a different leader — backs away from a strategy of financing data centers, then the AI boom itself loses momentum. The Washington Post reported on Thursday that recent actions by lawmakers suggest that more potentially damaging revelations about Nvidia could be in store as Huang is hauled before committees — and Democrats make the US administration's export control policies a central part of their tech oversight agenda next year. 'Warring States period' Some industry insiders believe that Huang's departure could have ripple effects across the global AI industry, introducing new uncertainties into the competitive landscape. Liu Shaoshan said Huang's departure could prompt major technology companies to accelerate the development of their own chips and diversify their computing architectures. "More importantly, the AI industry is shifting from large language model training toward large-scale inference and embodied AI. Future competition will gradually move beyond computing power alone to encompass computing architectures, software ecosystems and application costs. This development could usher in a 'Warring States period' for the chip industry," the expert said. Liu Shaoshan further noted that the "Warring States period" refers to a scenario in which multiple players compete for dominance in the chip industry. Established industry giants will begin to see their advantages challenged by new technologies and emerging demands, while different computing architectures will gain fresh opportunities to compete, he said, noting that domestic chip industries in some countries will also have new opportunities for development. For companies around the world, this could be one of the most important industrial opportunities of the next decade, Liu Shaoshan said. Future competition will no longer be simply about whose chips offer greater computing power, but about who can anticipate the direction of next-generation AI development earlier and build the computing architectures, software ecosystems and supply chains to support it, he said. Those that seize the opportunities presented by this wave of technological change could emerge as the next global chip giants. Meanwhile, An Bo said that some chipmakers will gain more opportunities to enter customers' supply chains.

item.title: China strictly prohibits all forms of surrogacy, violations will face severe legal penalties: official
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 16:49:00
Photo: VCG China strictly prohibits all forms of surrogacy, and organizing surrogacy constitutes a criminal offense, violates ethical norms, and will be subject to severe legal penalties, National Health Commission spokesperson Yang Jinrui said on Friday. So-called "surrogacy agreements" are not protected by law, and those involved may also be held legally accountable, according to the spokesperson. Some localities in China have reported cases involving surrogacy or the alleged illegal use of assisted reproductive technologies. For example, CCTV News reported that health and public security authorities in Changsha, Central China's Hunan Province, raided two underground facilities illegally providing assisted reproductive services in the city's Yuelu district on October 29, detaining 21 people suspected of involvement in illegal surrogacy and seizing drugs and medical equipment. Global Times

item.title: It's Jensen Huang today. Who is next? Washington's list of targets may keep growing
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 11:33:00
Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang Photo: VCG Jensen Huang, one of the most prominent figures in the global AI boom, has resigned. The immediate trigger, as presented in public, was a series of reports about his private life. But from the initial reports in the New York Times to the intense coverage across US media, the controversy has become about far more than a personal matter. Huang's affair was framed from the outset as a matter of US national security. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote in an X post, "Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." This is a pattern worth watching closely amid the current US climate of technological competition with China. First, an individual case is used to ignite public debate; then the framework of "national security" is invoked to elevate it into an issue of systemic risk. In today's Washington, "national security" can sometimes be invoked without reference to a concrete, verifiable threat, becoming a narrative tool that can be applied to prominent ethnic Chinese professionals operating at the intersection of US-China tech competition. The Huang case illustrates this pattern starkly: he lobbied for chip exports to China - a move that could be portrayed as potentially endangering national security; he reportedly had a personal relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of having ties to Chinese intelligence - another "potential national security concern;" and he wielded influence in Washington while maintaining business ties with China - again, grounds for raising "national security concerns." The word "may" is the key. It allows suspicion to be cast without establishing that wrongdoing has occurred or reaching a verdict. In this climate, a combination of Chinese identity and political circumstances can be enough to turn a celebrated business leader into a perceived security risk. The more accomplished and influential a person is, and the more centrally positioned they are between China and the US, the more vulnerable they may become to being singled out in the name of "national security." More alarming is the way this is reinforced by a broader narrative that demonizes China. China is cast as a strategic competitor of the US, while "national security precautions" imposed on the entire Chinese community are being heightened to an unprecedented degree. "The Jensen Huang affair exposes corporate America's China problem" - read a headline by The Hill. But this problem was not created by China; it reflects a contradiction within the US itself. On one hand, the US relies on the creativity and expertise of top Chinese talent; on the other, it increasingly treats them as potential security threats. It needs Nvidia's technology and global competitiveness, yet it does not want the company to make its own commercial decisions about the Chinese market. That is the real contradiction. This contradiction will not stop with Jensen Huang alone. The next target could well be other tech entrepreneurs unwilling to fully align with Washington's political agenda - including those who might argue that the US should win by running faster rather than by tripping up its opponents. In the current US political environment, ordinary business logic has come to be seen as "politically incorrect." Entrepreneurs are being forced to fight on two fronts at once: the technology race in the global market, and political scrutiny in Washington. Many in Silicon Valley will probably have to weigh every decision carefully: asking not whether they have done anything wrong, but whether their business decisions involving China and the US might one day be recast as "national security risks." It's Jensen Huang today. Who is next? Perhaps Washington is already looking for the answer.

item.title: Why becoming a 'gatekeeper' for US protectionism is not in Mexico's interest
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 00:27:00
US Mexico Illustration: Xia Qing/GT Washington has erected a wall of protectionism around the globe, and Mexico is eager to pass it more bricks, helping plug the "loopholes." But the higher this wall rises, the more likely it is to hem in Mexico itself, constraining not only its development prospects but also its independence in shaping trade policy. According to Reuters, Luis Rosendo Gutierrez, Mexico's deputy economy minister for foreign trade, said on Wednesday that the Mexican government had tightened traceability measures with industry to ensure that no steel from China or other countries is rerouted through its territory into the US by exploiting Mexico's trade preferences. Meanwhile, Mexico is urging Washington to ease tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and automobiles. Jiang Shixue, a distinguished professor at Hangzhou Normal University, told the Global Times that Mexico's move is rooted in its economic predicament created by strong dependence on the US. Facing US tariff pressure and uncertainty surrounding the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement review, Mexico hopes that aligning itself with Washington's restrictions on trade with China will win concessions from the US. Since 2025, Mexico has repeatedly followed the US to announce measures to impose tariffs on imports from China and other countries without free-trade agreements. It seems that Mexico is actively standing guard at the door on Washington's behalf. While other countries may justify trade barriers as necessary to protect their own industries, Mexico's restrictions appear to be protecting the interests of a "third party." In effect, Mexico risks turning itself into a gatekeeper for Washington's protectionism. This could end up as a potential "Faustian bargain." Mexico hopes to sacrifice part of its economic and trade cooperation with China in exchange for US concessions on tariffs and trade. But it may discover that what it surrenders far outweighs what it could gain. On the one hand, Washington is unlikely to abandon its trade pressure on Mexico. On the other, Mexico risks sacrificing long-term industrial cooperation, supply chain diversification and, ultimately, its economic sovereignty. According to Gutierrez, the country has already reduced steel and aluminum imports from countries including China, South Korea and India, by about 30 percent. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, pointed out that manufacturing is a pillar of Mexico's economy, and steel and aluminum are essential inputs for industries such as auto manufacturing and machinery. Cutting imports of these materials could further aggravate supply pressures on Mexican manufacturers, disrupting production and undermining supply chain stability. More importantly, if Mexico can readily change its trade policies under external pressure, other countries may begin to question the stability and predictability of its investment and trade environment, he added. Once policy predictability is undermined, the price Mexico pays could go far beyond the immediate costs of tariffs. Just one day before the report, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum stressed that respect for sovereignty and cooperation free from subordination "are non-negotiable" tenets of Mexico's relations with the US. True sovereignty should not be confined to political rhetoric. It should be reflected in a country's ability to independently choose its trading partners, allocate resources according to its development needs and formulate its own economic and trade policies. In an increasingly interconnected global economy, broader international partnerships give countries greater room to maneuver amid external uncertainties. Canada, also deeply integrated into the North American economic system, has not abandoned efforts to diversify its trading partners and is actively seeking to expand cooperation with China and other economies to get rid of its dependence on the US. America's trade wall is America's choice. Mexico has no reason to turn it into its own barrier to development. What Mexico truly needs is not to become another brick in Washington's protectionist wall, but to safeguard its economic sovereignty, preserve its ability to connect with global markets and participate in international industrial chains. Otherwise, in trying to please Washington, Mexico risks cutting off its nose to spite its face.

item.title: Dancing to their own beat
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-12 23:38:00
Members of a rural women's dance group perform in Linzhou, Central China's Henan Province, on March 6, 2026. The group, which has been getting a lot of attention online, gathers almost every afternoon to livestream their dance performances. Photo: VCG What do older people in rural areas do with their days? Work the fields, look after grandchildren or simply sit in the sun and reminisce? In a courtyard in Linzhou, Central China's Henan Province, a lively beat fills the air. A group of rural women averaging around 55 years of age stretch and sway with bright smiles as they livestream themselves dancing, attracting thousands of viewers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Farm work and housework chores fill their days; dancing on livestream offers a fleeting respite that belongs to them alone. This once-niche form of rural livestreaming has become more than just an online sensation. It is an attempt by older people to reclaim a sense of self and a vivid reflection of the changing cultural life in rural China. Another way to live Nearly 60-year-old Jiao Jianyu is the dance group's front-and-center performer. During live streams, she often appears in red, dancing with unmatched fervor, and is frequently singled out by online viewers as the group's standout performer. "Jiao is a natural-born dancer. She can pick up a dance after watching it just once or twice, and there's natural spark and energy in her movements," Chen Hongyu, founder of the rural woman dancing group, told the Global Times. Off camera, however, Jiao's life is very different. Her husband works as a migrant laborer in the city, leaving her to shoulder the burden of farm work and care for elderly family members and children at home. Her 35-year-old son has an intellectual disability and a cognitive development level comparable to that of a three-year-old, requiring constant care to keep him safe. It was only after a fan asked if something was troubling her that she began making a conscious effort to smile and appear more cheerful on camera. Since then, fans have cheered her on, with her infectious laughter filling the air. That kind of encouragement, she told the Global Times, is like warm sunshine, easing the hardships of daily life and giving her "fresh motivation to carry on." Jiao also helps organize the dancers' formations and decide the order of performances during livestreams. She knows the entire dance routine and has a keen eye for the personalities and strengths of local women hoping to join the group. "Those in the front row need to have good memories, since everyone behind follows their lead. Those with a knack for humor help liven things up and draw viewers in," she said shyly. Asked how livestream dancing had changed her life the most, she said, "These broadcasts give me a change of scenery, allowing me to break free from the tedious, unrelenting routine of housework." Jiao is not alone in finding a new sense of purpose through dancing. Zhang Ruifang, who is always seen smiling on camera, lost her son late last year. He had loved dancing and, before he passed away, encouraged his mother to do what she loved. His encouragement prompted Zhang to take up dancing, helping her cope with her grief. Jiao recalled Zhang telling the group that dancing made her feel as though her son were still by her side, with every step bringing back memories of him. Li Ying, 55, has also found solace through the group. For years, her mother, who has Alzheimer's disease, required round-the-clock care, leaving Li largely housebound. That changed once the livestreams started. Now she brings her mother along to the dance sessions. The older woman seems to enjoy the lively atmosphere, and her mood has noticeably brightened. For Li, the change has brought some much-needed relief after years of caregiving. "Life has dealt me its hardships and burdens, yet I refuse to wallow in self-pity. Life is not just about getting by. It's about finding joy," Li said. Chen explained that most of these women, facing age-related and other barriers, struggle to find work outside the village. Meanwhile, cultural and recreational activities in the village are few and far between. "When we first started the livestreams, we simply wanted to give them something to do and let them see that there is another way to live," he said. Bright glow Now, 40 to 50 older women take part in the livestreams each day. This informal dance group has attracted more than 270,000 followers on Douyin, with its livestreams regularly drawing thousands of concurrent viewers. The women earn roughly 50 yuan ($7.50) a day through livestreaming. For them, that modest income means more than just money. "Dancing gives me something to look forward to every day, and I can also earn a little extra to help with household expenses," Jiao said. "It makes me feel that even at my age, I can still realize my own potential." The props they use add a homespun charm. Lion heads, colored balls and wooden horses are all handmade by the women themselves, reworked from discarded materials. The approach keeps costs down, but it also weaves local creativity into every performance, turning the props into a highlight of the livestream room. Although their dance moves lack professional polish and their choreography is simple, the women's unpretentious charm has struck a chord with many netizens. "They don't strive for perfection, they simply enjoy dancing. There's a warmth in their everyday lives that reminds me how ordinary people can make even the simplest lives shine," one netizen wrote. Jia Zhiwen, head of the village's Party committee, said livestreams have brought the village greater online visibility, while also challenging traditional stereotypes of rural women and enriching their spiritual lives during the agricultural off-season. As for the future, the troupe members have no grand plans. "Holding hope for tomorrow is the best plan of all," Jiao said.
